title: Hello, world
note: One sentence.
source: Say "Hello, world!"

title: FizzBuzz
note: Loops, branches and “is divisible by”.
source:
# FizzBuzz, from 1 to 100.

Let the count be 1.

Repeat 100 times:
  If the count is divisible by 15:
    Say "FizzBuzz"
  Otherwise if the count is divisible by 3:
    Say "Fizz"
  Otherwise if the count is divisible by 5:
    Say "Buzz"
  Otherwise:
    Say the count.
  Add 1 to the count.

For example, the count is 101.

title: Dragons, treasure and tax
note: Kinds, adjectives, worked-out properties, verbs and rules.
source:
# A small tale of dragons, treasure and tax.

# --- The glossary: what the words mean --------------------------------------

A dragon has an age (number).
A treasure has a worth (money) and an owner (dragon).
A knight has a purse (money) and a courage (number).

The hoard of a dragon is the total worth of its treasures.
The tax of a dragon is 10% of its hoard.

A dragon is ancient when its age is at least 500.
A dragon is poor when its hoard is less than $1,000.
A knight is brave when its courage is more than 5.

A knight's purse is never less than $0.
A treasure's worth is never less than $0.

# --- The cast ----------------------------------------------------------------

There is a dragon called Smaug whose age is 771.
There is a dragon called Norbert whose age is 1.

There is a treasure called Arkenstone whose worth is $9,000 and whose owner is Smaug.
There is a treasure called Goblet whose worth is $3,000 and whose owner is Smaug.
There is a treasure called Teaspoon whose worth is $40 and whose owner is Norbert.

There is a knight called Gawain whose purse is $300 and whose courage is 8.
There is a knight called Robin whose purse is $20 and whose courage is 2.

# --- Examples double as tests ------------------------------------------------

For example, the hoard of Smaug is $12,000.
For example, the tax of Smaug is $1,200.
For example, Smaug is ancient and Norbert is poor.

# --- Verbs -------------------------------------------------------------------

To send a knight against a dragon:
  If the knight is not brave:
    Say "{the knight's name} takes one look at {the dragon's name} and goes home."
  Otherwise if the dragon is poor:
    Say "{the knight's name} feels sorry for {the dragon's name} and leaves a coin."
    Subtract $1 from the knight's purse.
  Otherwise:
    Let the loot be the tax of the dragon.
    For each treasure of the dragon:
      Subtract 10% of the treasure's worth from the treasure's worth.
    Add the loot to the knight's purse.
    Say "{the knight's name} collects {the loot} in tax from {the dragon's name}."

To give a treasure to a dragon:
  Say "{the treasure's name} changes claws: {the treasure's owner's name} to {the dragon's name}."
  Set the treasure's owner to the dragon.

# --- The story ---------------------------------------------------------------

Say "-- Roll call --"
For each dragon:
  Say "{its name}, aged {its age}, sits on {its hoard}."

Say ""
Say "-- Tax season --"
Send Robin against Smaug.
Send Gawain against Norbert.
Send Gawain against Smaug.
Say "Gawain rides home with {Gawain's purse}."

For example, the hoard of Smaug is $10,800.
For example, Gawain's purse is $1,499.

Say ""
Say "-- A gift --"
Give Goblet to Norbert.
For example, Norbert is not poor.

Say ""
Say "-- Four hundred years pass --"
Repeat 400 times:
  For each dragon:
    Add 1 to its age.

For each dragon:
  If it is ancient:
    Say "{its name} is now {its age} and ancient. Treasures: {the number of its treasures}, worth {its hoard}."
  Otherwise:
    Say "{its name} is {its age}: still a youngster. Treasures: {the number of its treasures}, worth {its hoard}."

Say ""
Say "Ancient dragons: {the number of ancient dragons} of {the number of dragons}."
Say "Treasures worth more than $1,000: {the number of treasures whose worth is more than $1,000}."
Say "All the treasure in the world: {the total worth of all treasures}."

title: Late fees
note: The same structures in a business setting.
source:
# Late fees: the same structures, in a less fanciful setting.

A customer has an email (text) and a balance (money).
An invoice has an amount (money), a due day (number), and a payer (customer).

Let today be 20.

An invoice is overdue when its due day is less than today.
The late fee of an invoice is 5% of its amount.
A customer is late when the number of overdue invoices of the customer is more than 0.

A customer's balance is never less than $0.

There is a customer called Ada whose email is "ada@example.com" and whose balance is $0.
There is a customer called Grace whose email is "grace@example.com" and whose balance is $0.

There is an invoice called Hosting whose amount is $200, whose due day is 5, and whose payer is Ada.
There is an invoice called Design whose amount is $1,500, whose due day is 18, and whose payer is Ada.
There is an invoice called Coffee whose amount is $40, whose due day is 25, and whose payer is Grace.

To remind a customer:
  For each overdue invoice of the customer:
    Add the late fee of the invoice to the customer's balance.
    Say "  {the invoice's name}: {the invoice's amount} was due on day {the invoice's due day}."
  Say "To {the customer's email}: you now owe {the customer's balance} in late fees."

For each late customer:
  Remind the customer.

For example, Ada's balance is $85.
For example, Grace is not late.

title: A tournament
note: Values that may be missing, worked-out values, and leaving early.
source:
# A tournament: values that may be missing, working out a value, and leaving early.

A horse has a speed (number).
A knight has a courage (number), a purse (money), and a mount (horse, if any).
A knight can be entered.

There is a horse called Shadowfax whose speed is 40.
There is a horse called Bill whose speed is 12.

There is a knight called Gawain whose courage is 8, whose purse is $300, and whose mount is Shadowfax.
There is a knight called Robin whose courage is 2, whose purse is $20, and whose mount is Bill.
There is a knight called Kay whose courage is 6 and whose purse is $90.

Let the entry fee always be $25.

# A knight on foot scores on courage alone. After the first "If", the compiler
# knows the knight has a mount, so the mount's speed can be used.

To work out the score (number) of a knight:
  If the knight has no mount:
    The answer is the knight's courage.
  The answer is the knight's courage * 10 + the knight's mount's speed.

To enter a knight:
  If the knight's purse is less than the entry fee:
    Say "{the knight} cannot pay the fee."
    Stop.
  Subtract the entry fee from the knight's purse.
  Now the knight is entered.
  Say "{the knight} enters with a score of {the score of the knight}."

# Only a knight who paid the fee can win. If none did, there is no champion.
To work out the champion (knight, if any):
  Let the best (knight, if any) be nothing.
  Let the top be 0.
  For each entered knight:
    If the score of the knight is more than the top:
      Set the best to the knight.
      Set the top to the score of the knight.
  The answer is the best.

For example, the score of Gawain is 120.
For example, the score of Kay is 6.

For each knight:
  Enter the knight.

Let the winner be the champion.
If the winner is nothing:
  Say "Nobody entered."
  End the program.

If the winner has a mount:
  Say "{the winner} wins, riding {the winner's mount}."
Otherwise:
  Say "{the winner} wins on foot."

title: A shaded triangle
note: The steps of a Vulkan program, drawn in characters.
source:
# Hello Triangle, in the shape of a Vulkan program.
#
# This is NOT the real Vulkan API, and it uses no graphics card. (For the real
# thing, see gpu_triangle.english.) The program follows the objects and steps of
# a Vulkan "hello triangle", and does the graphics card's work itself: it finds
# which points are inside the triangle, shades each one, and draws with
# characters. Each step is marked with the Vulkan call it stands for.
#
#   python -m englishscript examples/triangle.english

# --- The objects Vulkan has you create ------------------------------------------

An instance has an application (text).
A device has an owner (instance).
A swapchain has a width (number), a height (number), and a device (device).
A pass has a background (text).
A pipeline has a pass (pass) and a target (swapchain).

# A vertex carries a position and a colour, as in the vertex buffer of the
# usual example. Positions run from -1 to 1, with y pointing down.
A vertex has an x (number), a y (number), a red (number), a green (number), and a blue (number).
A triangle has a top corner (vertex), a right corner (vertex), and a left corner (vertex).

# The terminal has no colours here, so a colour is shown by how bright it is.
The glow of a vertex is 0.2126 * its red + 0.7152 * its green + 0.0722 * its blue.

# --- The vertex shader, and the viewport ------------------------------------------
# Where a vertex lands on the screen, in characters across and lines down.

To work out the column (number) of a vertex on a screen (swapchain):
  The answer is (the vertex's x + 1) / 2 * the screen's width.

To work out the row (number) of a vertex on a screen (swapchain):
  The answer is (the vertex's y + 1) / 2 * the screen's height.

# --- The rasteriser ---------------------------------------------------------------
# How far a point lies to one side of the line from one vertex to another.
# The graphics card does this for every point of the screen.

To work out the edge (number) from a tail (vertex) to a head (vertex) at a px (number) by a py (number) on a screen (swapchain):
  Let tx be the column of the tail on the screen.
  Let ty be the row of the tail on the screen.
  Let hx be the column of the head on the screen.
  Let hy be the row of the head on the screen.
  The answer is (the px - tx) * (hy - ty) - (the py - ty) * (hx - tx).

# --- The fragment shader ----------------------------------------------------------
# The glow at one point: each corner's glow, in proportion to how near the point
# is to that corner. A point outside the triangle has no fragment at all.

To work out the fragment (number, if any) of a triangle at a px (number) by a py (number) on a screen (swapchain):
  Let the top be the triangle's top corner.
  Let the right be the triangle's right corner.
  Let the left be the triangle's left corner.
  Let wx be the column of the left on the screen.
  Let wy be the row of the left on the screen.
  Let the area be the edge from the top to the right at wx by wy on the screen.
  Let the top share be the edge from the right to the left at the px by the py on the screen / the area.
  Let the right share be the edge from the left to the top at the px by the py on the screen / the area.
  Let the left share be the edge from the top to the right at the px by the py on the screen / the area.
  If the top share is less than 0 or the right share is less than 0 or the left share is less than 0:
    The answer is nothing.
  The answer is the top share * the top's glow + the right share * the right's glow + the left share * the left's glow.

# --- The surface format -----------------------------------------------------------
# Which character stands for a glow.

To work out the mark (text) for a level (number):
  If the level is less than 0.12:
    The answer is ".".
  If the level is less than 0.19:
    The answer is ":".
  If the level is less than 0.26:
    The answer is "-".
  If the level is less than 0.34:
    The answer is "=".
  If the level is less than 0.42:
    The answer is "+".
  If the level is less than 0.50:
    The answer is "*".
  If the level is less than 0.58:
    The answer is "#".
  If the level is less than 0.66:
    The answer is "%".
  The answer is "@".

# --- Drawing (vkCmdDraw), one line of the screen at a time ------------------------

To draw a triangle with a pipeline:
  Let the screen be the pipeline's target.
  Let down be 0.
  Repeat the screen's height times:
    Let the line be "".
    Let across be 0.
    Repeat the screen's width times:
      Let the light be the fragment of the triangle at (across + 0.5) by (down + 0.5) on the screen.
      If the light is nothing:
        Set the line to "{the line}{the pipeline's pass's background}".
      Otherwise:
        Set the line to "{the line}{the mark for the light}".
      Add 1 to across.
    Say the line.
    Add 1 to down.

# --- The program: the same steps a Vulkan program takes ---------------------------

# vkCreateInstance
There is an instance called Loader whose application is "Hello Triangle".

# vkCreateDevice
There is a device called Card whose owner is Loader.

# vkCreateSwapchainKHR: the screen is 60 characters by 30 lines of the terminal.
There is a swapchain called Terminal whose width is 60, whose height is 30, and whose device is Card.

# vkCreateRenderPass: what the screen is cleared to.
There is a pass called Clear whose background is " ".

# vkCreateGraphicsPipelines
There is a pipeline called Painter whose pass is Clear and whose target is Terminal.

# The vertex buffer: red at the top, green at the right, blue at the left.
There is a vertex called Apex whose x is 0, whose y is -0.5, whose red is 1, whose green is 0, and whose blue is 0.
There is a vertex called East whose x is 0.5, whose y is 0.5, whose red is 0, whose green is 1, and whose blue is 0.
There is a vertex called West whose x is -0.5, whose y is 0.5, whose red is 0, whose green is 0, and whose blue is 1.
There is a triangle called Hello whose top corner is Apex, whose right corner is East, and whose left corner is West.

# Examples double as tests. The arithmetic is exact, so the middle of the
# triangle glows by exactly one third: an equal share of each corner.
For example, the column of Apex on Terminal is 30.
For example, the row of Apex on Terminal is 7.5.
For example, the fragment of Hello at 0 by 0 on Terminal is nothing.
For example, (the fragment of Hello at 30 by 17.5 on Terminal) or else 0 is 1 / 3.

# vkCmdDraw and vkQueuePresentKHR
Say "{Loader's application}, drawn on {Card}:"
Draw Hello with Painter.

title: A to-do list
note: It asks for commands. Try: add Buy milk, done 1, list, quit.
source:
# A to-do list that remembers itself between runs.
#
#   python -m englishscript examples/todo.english
#
# Commands: list, add <title>, done <number>, undo <number>, remove <number>, clear, quit.
# The list is kept in todo.txt, in the folder the program is run from.

A task has a position (number).
A task can be done.

Let the save file always be "todo.txt".
Let the next position be 1.

# --- Working things out ---------------------------------------------------------

# "add Buy milk" from 4 is "Buy milk".
To work out the rest (text) of a line (text) from a start (number):
  The answer is the last (the length of the line - the start) letters of the line.

To work out the match (task, if any) for a pick (number):
  For each task whose position is the pick:
    The answer is the task.
  The answer is nothing.

# "2" is the task in position 2. Anything that is not a number is no task.
To work out the choice (task, if any) from a phrase (text):
  Let the pick be the phrase as a number.
  If the pick is nothing:
    The answer is nothing.
  The answer is the match for the pick.

# --- Verbs -----------------------------------------------------------------------

To renumber:
  Set the next position to 1.
  For each task:
    Set the task's position to the next position.
    Add 1 to the next position.

# Each line of the file is "x " or "- " followed by the title. Anything else,
# such as a line someone typed in by hand with no title, is passed over.
To load:
  Try:
    For each line in the lines of the file the save file:
      If the length of the line is less than 3:
        Skip this line.
      If the line starts with "x ":
        Let the entry be a new task called the rest of the line from 2 whose position is the next position.
        Now the entry is done.
        Add 1 to the next position.
      Otherwise if the line starts with "- ":
        There is a new task called the rest of the line from 2 whose position is the next position.
        Add 1 to the next position.
  If that fails:
    Say "No saved list yet. Starting a new one."

To save:
  Write "" to the file the save file.
  For each task:
    If the task is done:
      Add "x {the task}{new line}" to the file the save file.
    Otherwise:
      Add "- {the task}{new line}" to the file the save file.

To show:
  If the number of tasks is 0:
    Say "Nothing to do."
    Stop.
  For each task:
    If the task is done:
      Say "  {the task's position}. [x] {the task}"
    Otherwise:
      Say "  {the task's position}. [ ] {the task}"
  Say "{the number of done tasks} of {the number of tasks} done."

# --- The program -----------------------------------------------------------------

Load.
Say "To-do list. Commands: list, add <title>, done <number>, undo <number>, remove <number>, clear, quit."
Show.

Let finished (yes or no) be no.
While finished is no:
  Ask ">" and let the command (text) be the reply.

  If the command is "quit":
    Set finished to yes.

  Otherwise if the command is "list":
    Show.

  Otherwise if the command starts with "add ":
    Let the title be the rest of the command from 4.
    If the title is "":
      Say "Add what?"
    Otherwise:
      There is a new task called the title whose position is the next position.
      Add 1 to the next position.
      Save.
      Say "Added: {the title}"

  Otherwise if the command starts with "done ":
    Let the words be the rest of the command from 5.
    Let the chosen be the choice from the words.
    If the chosen is nothing:
      Say "There is no task with that number."
    Otherwise:
      Now the chosen is done.
      Save.
      Say "Done: {the chosen}"

  Otherwise if the command starts with "undo ":
    Let the words be the rest of the command from 5.
    Let the chosen be the choice from the words.
    If the chosen is nothing:
      Say "There is no task with that number."
    Otherwise:
      Now the chosen is not done.
      Save.
      Say "Not done: {the chosen}"

  Otherwise if the command starts with "remove ":
    Let the words be the rest of the command from 7.
    Let the chosen be the choice from the words.
    If the chosen is nothing:
      Say "There is no task with that number."
    Otherwise:
      Say "Removed: {the chosen}"
      Remove the chosen.
      Renumber.
      Save.

  Otherwise if the command is "clear":
    For each done task:
      Remove the task.
    Renumber.
    Save.
    Show.

  Otherwise:
    Say "I don't know that. Try: list, add <title>, done <number>, undo <number>, remove <number>, clear, quit."

Say "Goodbye."

title: SHA-256 from first principles
note: It takes a few seconds to set up, then asks for text to hash.
source:
# SHA-256, worked out from first principles.
#
#   python -m englishscript examples/sha256.english
#
# EnglishScript has no bit operators, no remainders, no rounding and no arrays.
# This program builds all of them from what the language does have: exact whole
# numbers of any size, halving, and "is divisible by".
#
#   - A number's lowest bit is whether it is divisible by 2. Halving it shifts
#     every bit one place to the right; doubling shifts them to the left.
#   - An array is a kind of thing with a place and a value.
#   - SHA-256's 72 constants are not typed in. They are the first 32 bits after
#     the point of the cube roots and square roots of the first primes, and the
#     program finds the primes and takes the roots itself.

Let the alphabet always be " !""#$%&'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ[\]^_`abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz{{|}}~".
Let the hex digits always be "0123456789abcdef".
Let the digest be "".

# --- Five arrays, as things -----------------------------------------------------------

A constant has a place (number) and a value (number).     # the 64 round constants
A seed has a place (number) and a value (number).         # the 8 starting values
A register has a place (number) and a value (number).     # the 8 running values
An entry has a place (number) and a value (number).       # the 64 words of the schedule
A byte has a place (number) and a value (number).         # the message, padded

To work out the key (number) at a spot (number):
  For each constant whose place is the spot:
    The answer is the constant's value.
  The answer is 0.

To work out the origin (number) at a spot (number):
  For each seed whose place is the spot:
    The answer is the seed's value.
  The answer is 0.

To work out the word (number) at a spot (number):
  For each entry whose place is the spot:
    The answer is the entry's value.
  The answer is 0.

To store an amount (number) at a spot (number):
  For each entry whose place is the spot:
    Set the entry's value to the amount.

# --- Bits, built from halving ---------------------------------------------------------

# Keep a number within 32 bits: take away 2 to the power 32 until it fits.
To work out the wrap (number) of a value (number):
  Let the rest be the value.
  While the rest is at least 4,294,967,296:
    Subtract 4,294,967,296 from the rest.
  The answer is the rest.

# The lowest bits of a number, as a number: its remainder on dividing by a power of two.
To work out the low part (number) of a value (number) under a width (number):
  Let the rest be the value.
  Let the part be 0.
  Let the unit be 1.
  Repeat the width times:
    If the rest is not divisible by 2:
      Add the unit to the part.
      Subtract 1 from the rest.
    Divide the rest by 2.
    Multiply the unit by 2.
  The answer is the part.

# Shift right: drop the lowest bit and halve, so many times.
To work out the slide (number) of a value (number) by a count (number):
  Let the rest be the value.
  Repeat the count times:
    If the rest is not divisible by 2:
      Subtract 1 from the rest.
    Divide the rest by 2.
  The answer is the rest.

# Rotate right within 32 bits: a bit that falls off the bottom comes back at the top.
To work out the turn (number) of a value (number) by a count (number):
  Let the rest be the value.
  Repeat the count times:
    If the rest is divisible by 2:
      Divide the rest by 2.
    Otherwise:
      Set the rest to (the rest - 1) / 2 + 2,147,483,648.
  The answer is the rest.

# Exclusive-or of three numbers: a bit is set where one or all three of them have it.
To work out the blend (number) of a left (number) with a middle (number) against a right (number):
  Let p be the left.
  Let q be the middle.
  Let r be the right.
  Let the result be 0.
  Let the unit be 1.
  Repeat 32 times:
    Let the ayes be 0.
    If p is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from p.
    If q is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from q.
    If r is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from r.
    If the ayes is 1 or the ayes is 3:
      Add the unit to the result.
    Divide p by 2.
    Divide q by 2.
    Divide r by 2.
    Multiply the unit by 2.
  The answer is the result.

# Majority: a bit is set where at least two of the three numbers have it.
To work out the vote (number) of a left (number) with a middle (number) against a right (number):
  Let p be the left.
  Let q be the middle.
  Let r be the right.
  Let the result be 0.
  Let the unit be 1.
  Repeat 32 times:
    Let the ayes be 0.
    If p is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from p.
    If q is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from q.
    If r is not divisible by 2:
      Add 1 to the ayes.
      Subtract 1 from r.
    If the ayes is at least 2:
      Add the unit to the result.
    Divide p by 2.
    Divide q by 2.
    Divide r by 2.
    Multiply the unit by 2.
  The answer is the result.

# Choose: each bit of the chooser picks that bit from the upper number if it is
# set, and from the lower number if it is not. With bits as 0 and 1 this needs
# no "if": the chosen bit is  c * u + (1 - c) * w.
To work out the pick (number) of a chooser (number) from an upper (number) over a lower (number):
  Let c be the chooser.
  Let u be the upper.
  Let w be the lower.
  Let the result be 0.
  Let the unit be 1.
  Repeat 32 times:
    Let the c bit be 0.
    Let the u bit be 0.
    Let the w bit be 0.
    If c is not divisible by 2:
      Set the c bit to 1.
      Subtract 1 from c.
    If u is not divisible by 2:
      Set the u bit to 1.
      Subtract 1 from u.
    If w is not divisible by 2:
      Set the w bit to 1.
      Subtract 1 from w.
    Add the unit * (the c bit * the u bit + (1 - the c bit) * the w bit) to the result.
    Divide c by 2.
    Divide u by 2.
    Divide w by 2.
    Multiply the unit by 2.
  The answer is the result.

# --- Primes and roots, for the constants ------------------------------------------------

To work out the primeness (yes or no) of a candidate (number):
  Let the divisor be 2.
  While the divisor * the divisor is at most the candidate:
    If the candidate is divisible by the divisor:
      The answer is no.
    Add 1 to the divisor.
  The answer is yes.

# The whole part of a root, found by halving the gap between a number that is
# too small and one that is too big. Everything stays a whole number.
To work out the root (number) of a target (number) with a degree (number):
  Let the floor be 0.
  Let the ceiling be 68,719,476,736.
  While the ceiling - the floor is more than 1:
    Let the middle be the floor + the ceiling.
    If the middle is not divisible by 2:
      Subtract 1 from the middle.
    Divide the middle by 2.
    Let the power be 1.
    Repeat the degree times:
      Multiply the power by the middle.
    If the power is at most the target:
      Set the floor to the middle.
    Otherwise:
      Set the ceiling to the middle.
  The answer is the floor.

# --- Text ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To work out the symbol (text) at a spot (number) of a line (text):
  The answer is the first 1 letters of the last (the length of the line - the spot + 1) letters of the line.

# The number a keyboard character stands for (its ASCII code), or nothing.
To work out the code (number, if any) of a mark (text):
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat the length of the alphabet times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    If the symbol at the spot of the alphabet is the mark:
      The answer is the spot + 31.
  The answer is nothing.

# --- One block of 64 bytes ------------------------------------------------------------------

To raise a spot (number) by an amount (number):
  For each register whose place is the spot:
    Set the register's value to the wrap of (the register's value + the amount).

To work out the reading (number) at a spot (number):
  For each register whose place is the spot:
    The answer is the register's value.
  The answer is 0.

To crunch:
  # Stretch the block's 16 words into 64.
  Let t be 16.
  Repeat 48 times:
    Let the near be the word at (t - 15).
    Let the far be the word at (t - 2).
    Let the near stir be the blend of the turn of the near by 7 with the turn of the near by 18 against the slide of the near by 3.
    Let the far stir be the blend of the turn of the far by 17 with the turn of the far by 19 against the slide of the far by 10.
    Store the wrap of (the word at (t - 16) + the near stir + the word at (t - 7) + the far stir) at t.
    Add 1 to t.

  # Sixty-four rounds of mixing.
  Let alpha be the reading at 0.
  Let beta be the reading at 1.
  Let gamma be the reading at 2.
  Let delta be the reading at 3.
  Let epsilon be the reading at 4.
  Let zeta be the reading at 5.
  Let eta be the reading at 6.
  Let theta be the reading at 7.
  Let the step be 0.
  Repeat 64 times:
    Let the upper stir be the blend of the turn of epsilon by 6 with the turn of epsilon by 11 against the turn of epsilon by 25.
    Let the chosen be the pick of epsilon from zeta over eta.
    Let the push be the wrap of (theta + the upper stir + the chosen + the key at the step + the word at the step).
    Let the lower stir be the blend of the turn of alpha by 2 with the turn of alpha by 13 against the turn of alpha by 22.
    Let the agreed be the vote of alpha with beta against gamma.
    Set theta to eta.
    Set eta to zeta.
    Set zeta to epsilon.
    Set epsilon to the wrap of (delta + the push).
    Set delta to gamma.
    Set gamma to beta.
    Set beta to alpha.
    Set alpha to the wrap of (the push + the lower stir + the agreed).
    Add 1 to the step.

  Raise 0 by alpha.
  Raise 1 by beta.
  Raise 2 by gamma.
  Raise 3 by delta.
  Raise 4 by epsilon.
  Raise 5 by zeta.
  Raise 6 by eta.
  Raise 7 by theta.

# --- The whole message --------------------------------------------------------------------

To hash a message (text):
  # The message as bytes.
  For each byte:
    Remove the byte.
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat the length of the message times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Let the found be the code of the symbol at the spot of the message.
    If the found is nothing:
      Fail because "I can only hash plain keyboard characters, and the one in place {the spot} is not."
    There is a new byte whose place is the spot and whose value is the found.

  # Padding: a single 1 bit, zeros, then the length in bits as eight bytes.
  Let the size be the spot + 1.
  There is a new byte whose place is the size and whose value is 128.
  While the size + 8 is not divisible by 64:
    Add 1 to the size.
    There is a new byte whose place is the size and whose value is 0.
  Let the bits be the spot * 8.
  Let the shift be 56.
  Repeat 8 times:
    Add 1 to the size.
    There is a new byte whose place is the size and whose value is the low part of (the slide of the bits by the shift) under 8.
    Subtract 8 from the shift.

  # Start from the seeds, then take the bytes four at a time into words, and
  # crunch every sixteen words. Shifting left by eight bits is multiplying by 256.
  For each register:
    Set the register's value to the origin at the register's place.
  Let the gathered be 0.
  Let the count be 0.
  Let the slot be 0.
  For each byte:
    Set the gathered to the gathered * 256 + the byte's value.
    Add 1 to the count.
    If the count is divisible by 4:
      Store the gathered at the slot.
      Set the gathered to 0.
      Add 1 to the slot.
      If the slot is 16:
        Crunch.
        Set the slot to 0.

  # The eight running values, written in hexadecimal, four bits at a time.
  Set the digest to "".
  For each register:
    Let the rest be the register's value.
    Let the piece be "".
    Repeat 8 times:
      Let the nibble be the low part of the rest under 4.
      Set the piece to "{the symbol at (the nibble + 1) of the hex digits}{the piece}".
      Set the rest to (the rest - the nibble) / 16.
    Set the digest to "{the digest}{the piece}".

# --- Setting up: the constants, from primes ------------------------------------------------

Let the cube scale be 1.
Repeat 96 times:
  Multiply the cube scale by 2.
Let the square scale be 1.
Repeat 64 times:
  Multiply the square scale by 2.

Let the prime be 2.
Let the tally be 0.
While the tally is less than 64:
  If the primeness of the prime is yes:
    There is a new constant whose place is the tally and whose value is the wrap of the root of (the prime * the cube scale) with 3.
    If the tally is less than 8:
      There is a new seed whose place is the tally and whose value is the wrap of the root of (the prime * the square scale) with 2.
      There is a new register whose place is the tally and whose value is 0.
    Add 1 to the tally.
  Add 1 to the prime.

Let the filled be 0.
Repeat 64 times:
  There is a new entry whose place is the filled and whose value is 0.
  Add 1 to the filled.

# The published constants, in decimal: 0x428a2f98, 0xc67178f2 and 0x6a09e667.
For example, the key at 0 is 1,116,352,408.
For example, the key at 63 is 3,329,325,298.
For example, the origin at 0 is 1,779,033,703.

# The bit operations, checked on small numbers.
For example, the slide of 200 by 3 is 25.
For example, the turn of 1 by 1 is 2,147,483,648.
For example, the low part of 1,000 under 4 is 8.
For example, the blend of 12 with 10 against 0 is 6.
For example, the vote of 12 with 10 against 6 is 14.
For example, the pick of 12 from 10 over 5 is 9.

# The published test values.
Hash "abc".
For example, the digest is "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad".
Hash "".
For example, the digest is "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855".

# --- The program ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Say "SHA-256, worked out in plain English. The constants and both test values check out."
Let finished (yes or no) be no.
While finished is no:
  Ask "Text to hash (leave it empty to finish):" and let the line (text) be the reply.
  If the line is "":
    Set finished to yes.
  Otherwise:
    Try:
      Hash the line.
      Say the digest.
    If that fails:
      Say "Sorry. {the problem}"

title: Primes and perfect numbers
note: Testing, listing and factoring, all built on “is divisible by”.
source:
# Primes: testing a number, listing them, taking a number apart, and perfect numbers.
#
# Everything here is built on one test: "is divisible by".

To work out the primeness (yes or no) of a candidate (number):
  If the candidate is less than 2:
    The answer is no.
  Let the divisor be 2.
  While the divisor * the divisor is at most the candidate:
    If the candidate is divisible by the divisor:
      The answer is no.
    Add 1 to the divisor.
  The answer is yes.

# Every prime up to a limit, as one line of text.
To work out the prime roll (text) to a limit (number):
  Let the line be "".
  Let n be 2.
  While n is at most the limit:
    If the primeness of n is yes:
      If the line is "":
        Set the line to "{n}".
      Otherwise:
        Set the line to "{the line}, {n}".
    Add 1 to n.
  The answer is the line.

# A number written as a product of primes: keep dividing by the smallest thing that divides it.
To work out the factoring (text) of a whole (number):
  Let the rest be the whole.
  Let the divisor be 2.
  Let the line be "".
  While the rest is more than 1:
    If the rest is divisible by the divisor:
      If the line is "":
        Set the line to "{the divisor}".
      Otherwise:
        Set the line to "{the line} x {the divisor}".
      Divide the rest by the divisor.
    Otherwise:
      Add 1 to the divisor.
  The answer is the line.

# A number is perfect when the numbers that divide it, itself aside, add up to it.
To work out the perfection (yes or no) of a whole (number):
  Let the sum be 0.
  Let d be 1.
  While d is less than the whole:
    If the whole is divisible by d:
      Add d to the sum.
    Add 1 to d.
  The answer is whether the sum is the whole.

For example, the primeness of 97 is yes.
For example, the primeness of 91 is no.
For example, the primeness of 1 is no.
For example, the factoring of 360 is "2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5".
For example, the perfection of 28 is yes.

Say "Primes to 60: {the prime roll to 60}."
Say "360 = {the factoring of 360}"
Say "1,001 = {the factoring of 1,001}"
Say "97 = {the factoring of 97}"

Let the tried be 2.
While the tried is less than 500:
  If the perfection of the tried is yes:
    Say "{the tried} is perfect."
  Add 1 to the tried.

title: Euclid’s greatest common measure
note: Two methods, by subtracting and by halving, and fractions in lowest terms.
source:
# Euclid: the greatest number that divides two others, found two ways.
#
# The language has no remainder, and neither had Euclid. His own method only
# takes the smaller from the larger until the two are equal. The second method
# is a modern one that only halves.

To work out the common measure (number) of a left (number) with a right (number):
  Let p be the left.
  Let q be the right.
  While p is not q:
    If p is more than q:
      Subtract q from p.
    Otherwise:
      Subtract p from q.
  The answer is p.

# Take out the twos the two numbers share. After that, halve whichever is even,
# and when both are odd, halve their difference.
To work out the halving measure (number) of a left (number) with a right (number):
  Let p be the left.
  Let q be the right.
  Let the twos be 1.
  While p is divisible by 2 and q is divisible by 2:
    Divide p by 2.
    Divide q by 2.
    Multiply the twos by 2.
  While p is not q:
    If p is divisible by 2:
      Divide p by 2.
    Otherwise if q is divisible by 2:
      Divide q by 2.
    Otherwise if p is more than q:
      Set p to (p - q) / 2.
    Otherwise:
      Set q to (q - p) / 2.
  The answer is p * the twos.

To work out the common multiple (number) of a left (number) with a right (number):
  The answer is the left * the right / the common measure of the left with the right.

# A fraction in its lowest terms, as text.
To work out the lowest terms (text) of a top (number) over a bottom (number):
  Let the shared be the common measure of the top with the bottom.
  The answer is "{the top / the shared}/{the bottom / the shared}".

For example, the common measure of 1,071 with 462 is 21.
For example, the halving measure of 1,071 with 462 is 21.
For example, the halving measure of 48 with 180 is 12.
For example, the common measure of 17 with 5 is 1.
For example, the common multiple of 4 with 6 is 12.
For example, the lowest terms of 462 over 1,071 is "22/51".

Say "The greatest number dividing 1,071 and 462 is {the common measure of 1,071 with 462}."
Say "By halving, it is {the halving measure of 1,071 with 462}."
Say "The least number that 21 and 6 both divide is {the common multiple of 21 with 6}."
Say "462/1,071 in lowest terms is {the lowest terms of 462 over 1,071}."

# Arithmetic is exact, so a third and a sixth really do make a half.
For example, 1 / 3 + 1 / 6 is 1 / 2.
Say "One third and one sixth make {1 / 3 + 1 / 6}."

title: Fibonacci numbers
note: A loop, a definition that uses itself, and a number of twenty-one digits.
source:
# Fibonacci numbers: each is the sum of the two before it.
#
# Numbers here are exact however large they grow, so the hundredth is no trouble.

To work out the fibonacci (number) at a place (number):
  Let the earlier be 0.
  Let the later be 1.
  Repeat the place times:
    Let the following be the earlier + the later.
    Set the earlier to the later.
    Set the later to the following.
  The answer is the earlier.

# The same thing, said the way the definition says it. It uses itself twice,
# so it is slow, and only fit for small places.
To work out the slow fibonacci (number) at a place (number):
  If the place is less than 2:
    The answer is the place.
  The answer is the slow fibonacci at (the place - 1) + the slow fibonacci at (the place - 2).

For example, the fibonacci at 10 is 55.
For example, the slow fibonacci at 15 is the fibonacci at 15.
For example, the fibonacci at 100 is 354,224,848,179,261,915,075.

Let the place be 1.
Let the line be "".
Repeat 15 times:
  Set the line to "{the line}{the fibonacci at the place} ".
  Add 1 to the place.
Say "The first fifteen: {the line}"
Say "The hundredth: {the fibonacci at 100}"

# The ratio of neighbours settles on the golden ratio.
Say "The 41st over the 40th: {the fibonacci at 41 / the fibonacci at 40}"

# The even ones below four million, added up.
Let the earlier be 1.
Let the later be 2.
Let the total be 0.
While the earlier is less than 4,000,000:
  If the earlier is divisible by 2:
    Add the earlier to the total.
  Let the following be the earlier + the later.
  Set the earlier to the later.
  Set the later to the following.
Say "The even ones below four million add up to {the total}."
For example, the total is 4,613,732.

title: Square roots and pi
note: Exact fractions: Heron’s method, a search by halving, and Machin’s formula.
source:
# Square roots and pi, by exact arithmetic.
#
# A number here is an exact fraction, never a rounded one. That makes two old
# methods easy to follow, because nothing is lost along the way. Only what is
# said is rounded, to four places.

# Heron's method: take a guess, and average it with the number divided by it.
# Each round roughly doubles the number of correct digits.
To work out the heron root (number) of a square (number) over a count (number):
  Let the guess be the square.
  Repeat the count times:
    Set the guess to (the guess + the square / the guess) / 2.
  The answer is the guess.

# The whole part of a square root, found by halving the gap between a number
# that is too small and one that is too big.
To work out the whole root (number) of a square (number):
  Let the floor be 0.
  Let the ceiling be the square + 1.
  While the ceiling - the floor is more than 1:
    Let the middle be the floor + the ceiling.
    If the middle is not divisible by 2:
      Subtract 1 from the middle.
    Divide the middle by 2.
    If the middle * the middle is at most the square:
      Set the floor to the middle.
    Otherwise:
      Set the ceiling to the middle.
  The answer is the floor.

# The angle whose tangent is one over a number, by Gregory's series:
# 1/x - 1/(3 x^3) + 1/(5 x^5) - ...
To work out the arc (number) of a divisor (number) over a count (number):
  Let the sum be 0.
  Let the power be the divisor.
  Let the odd be 1.
  Let the sign be 1.
  Repeat the count times:
    Add the sign / (the odd * the power) to the sum.
    Multiply the power by the divisor * the divisor.
    Add 2 to the odd.
    Set the sign to 0 - the sign.
  The answer is the sum.

For example, the whole root of 144 is 12.
For example, the whole root of 150 is 12.
# Heron's guesses come down on 12 from above and never quite land on it, and
# an exact fraction does not pretend otherwise.
For example, the heron root of 144 over 10 is more than 12 and the heron root of 144 over 10 is less than 12.000001.

Let the root be the heron root of 2 over 6.
Say "The square root of 2 is about {the root}."
For example, the root * the root is more than 1.999999999999 and the root * the root is less than 2.000000000001.

# Thirty-one digits of it: the whole root of 2 followed by sixty noughts.
Let the scale be 1.
Repeat 60 times:
  Multiply the scale by 10.
Say "Its first thirty-one digits: {the whole root of (2 * the scale)}"
For example, the whole root of (2 * the scale) is 1,414,213,562,373,095,048,801,688,724,209.

# Machin's formula of 1706: pi is 16 arcs of 5, less 4 arcs of 239.
Let pi be 16 * the arc of 5 over 12 - 4 * the arc of 239 over 12.
Say "Pi is about {pi}."
For example, pi is more than 3.14159265358979 and pi is less than 3.1415926535898.

title: Sorting and searching
note: A row of things sorted by swapping, then searched by halving.
source:
# Sorting and searching.
#
# The language has no arrays, so a row of numbers is a row of things, each with
# a place and a value. Sorting is then swapping values between places.

A slot has a place (number) and a value (number).

There is a slot called One whose place is 1 and whose value is 42.
There is a slot called Two whose place is 2 and whose value is 7.
There is a slot called Three whose place is 3 and whose value is 93.
There is a slot called Four whose place is 4 and whose value is 18.
There is a slot called Five whose place is 5 and whose value is 61.
There is a slot called Six whose place is 6 and whose value is 3.
There is a slot called Seven whose place is 7 and whose value is 77.
There is a slot called Eight whose place is 8 and whose value is 25.

Let the swaps be 0.

To work out the holding (number) at a spot (number):
  For each slot whose place is the spot:
    The answer is the slot's value.
  The answer is 0.

To put an amount (number) at a spot (number):
  For each slot whose place is the spot:
    Set the slot's value to the amount.

To swap a near (number) with a far (number):
  Let the held be the holding at the near.
  Put the holding at the far at the near.
  Put the held at the far.
  Add 1 to the swaps.

To work out the row (text):
  Let the line be "".
  For each slot:
    Set the line to "{the line}{the slot's value} ".
  The answer is the line.

# Bubble sort: walk along the row swapping neighbours that are out of order,
# and stop after a walk that swaps nothing.
To sort:
  Let the size be the number of slots.
  Let settled (yes or no) be no.
  While settled is no:
    Set settled to yes.
    Let the spot be 1.
    Repeat the size - 1 times:
      If the holding at the spot is more than the holding at (the spot + 1):
        Swap the spot with the spot + 1.
        Set settled to no.
      Add 1 to the spot.

# Binary search: look at the middle of what is left, and throw away the half
# the number cannot be in. It gives the place, or nothing.
To work out the finding (number, if any) of a wanted (number):
  Let the low be 1.
  Let the high be the number of slots.
  While the low is at most the high:
    Let the middle be the low + the high.
    If the middle is not divisible by 2:
      Subtract 1 from the middle.
    Divide the middle by 2.
    If the holding at the middle is the wanted:
      The answer is the middle.
    If the holding at the middle is less than the wanted:
      Set the low to the middle + 1.
    Otherwise:
      Set the high to the middle - 1.
  The answer is nothing.

Say "Before: {the row}"
Sort.
Say "After:  {the row}"
Say "That took {the swaps} swaps."
For example, the row is "3 7 18 25 42 61 77 93 ".
For example, the swaps is 14.

Let the found be the finding of 61.
If the found is nothing:
  Say "61 is not there."
Otherwise:
  Say "61 is in place {the found}."
Say "And 50? {the finding of 50}."
For example, (the finding of 61) or else 0 is 6.
For example, the finding of 50 is nothing.

title: The Tower of Hanoi
note: A verb that uses itself, moving four discs in fifteen moves.
source:
# The Towers of Hanoi: a verb that uses itself.
#
# To move a stack of discs, move all but the biggest out of the way, move the
# biggest, then move the rest back on top of it. "Out of the way" is the same
# puzzle with one disc fewer, so the verb calls itself.

A peg has a height (number).

There is a peg called Oak whose height is 4.
There is a peg called Ash whose height is 0.
There is a peg called Elm whose height is 0.

Let the moves be 0.

To move a count (number) from a source (peg) to a target (peg) by a spare (peg):
  If the count is 0:
    Stop.
  Move the count - 1 from the source to the spare by the target.
  Subtract 1 from the source's height.
  Add 1 to the target's height.
  Add 1 to the moves.
  Say "{the moves}. Disc {the count} goes from {the source} to {the target}."
  Move the count - 1 from the spare to the target by the source.

Move 4 from Oak to Elm by Ash.

Say "Done in {the moves} moves."
For example, the moves is 15.
For example, Elm's height is 4 and Oak's height is 0 and Ash's height is 0.

# For n discs it always takes one less than two multiplied by itself n times.
To work out the fewest (number) for a count (number):
  Let the doubling be 1.
  Repeat the count times:
    Multiply the doubling by 2.
  The answer is the doubling - 1.

For example, the fewest for 4 is 15.
Say "Sixty-four discs, as in the legend, would take {the fewest for 64} moves."

title: The Collatz puzzle
note: While loops, skipping a round and stopping early.
source:
# The Collatz puzzle: halve a number if it is even, otherwise treble it and
# add one. Nobody has proved that this always comes down to 1, but it always has.

# How many steps a number takes to reach 1.
To work out the flight (number) of a start (number):
  Let n be the start.
  Let the steps be 0.
  While n is not 1:
    If n is divisible by 2:
      Divide n by 2.
    Otherwise:
      Set n to 3 * n + 1.
    Add 1 to the steps.
  The answer is the steps.

# The highest number reached on the way.
To work out the peak (number) of a start (number):
  Let n be the start.
  Let the top be the start.
  While n is not 1:
    If n is divisible by 2:
      Divide n by 2.
    Otherwise:
      Set n to 3 * n + 1.
    If n is more than the top:
      Set the top to n.
  The answer is the top.

For example, the flight of 1 is 0.
For example, the flight of 6 is 8.
For example, the flight of 27 is 111.
For example, the peak of 27 is 9,232.

# Which number below 30 takes longest? One loop, with a skip and an early stop.
Let the best be 1.
Let the longest be 0.
Let the tried be 0.
Repeat 1,000 times:
  Add 1 to the tried.
  If the tried is at least 30:
    Stop repeating.
  If the flight of the tried is at most the longest:
    Skip this round.
  Set the best to the tried.
  Set the longest to the flight of the tried.

Say "Below 30, the longest flight is {the longest} steps, from {the best}."
Say "On the way, {the best} climbs as high as {the peak of the best}."
For example, the best is 27.

title: A cipher and a palindrome
note: Taking text apart a letter at a time.
source:
# Working with text: a Caesar cipher, a palindrome test, and counting.
#
# The language cannot ask for a letter's number, so the alphabet is a piece of
# text, and a letter's number is its place in it.

Let the alphabet always be "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz".

To work out the symbol (text) at a spot (number) of a line (text):
  The answer is the first 1 letters of the last (the length of the line - the spot + 1) letters of the line.

# Where a letter stands in the alphabet, or nothing if it is not a letter.
To work out the standing (number, if any) of a mark (text):
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat 26 times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    If the symbol at the spot of the alphabet is the mark:
      The answer is the spot.
  The answer is nothing.

# One letter moved along the alphabet, going round at the end. Anything that is
# not a letter is left as it is.
To work out the turned (text) of a mark (text) by a shift (number):
  Let the spot be the standing of the mark.
  If the spot is nothing:
    The answer is the mark.
  Let the landing be the spot + the shift.
  While the landing is more than 26:
    Subtract 26 from the landing.
  While the landing is less than 1:
    Add 26 to the landing.
  The answer is the symbol at the landing of the alphabet.

To work out the cipher (text) of a message (text) by a shift (number):
  Let the plain be the message in lower case.
  Let the secret be "".
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat the length of the plain times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Set the secret to "{the secret}{the turned of the symbol at the spot of the plain by the shift}".
  The answer is the secret.

# Only the letters of a text, in lower case.
To work out the letters only (text) of a message (text):
  Let the plain be the message in lower case.
  Let the kept be "".
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat the length of the plain times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Let the mark be the symbol at the spot of the plain.
    If the standing of the mark is not nothing:
      Set the kept to "{the kept}{the mark}".
  The answer is the kept.

To work out the backwards (text) of a message (text):
  Let the reversed be "".
  Let the spot be 0.
  Repeat the length of the message times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Set the reversed to "{the symbol at the spot of the message}{the reversed}".
  The answer is the reversed.

# A palindrome reads the same both ways, once spaces and punctuation are set aside.
To work out the mirroring (yes or no) of a message (text):
  Let the bare be the letters only of the message.
  The answer is whether the bare is the backwards of the bare.

Let the order be "Attack at dawn, by the old bridge!".
Let the hidden be the cipher of the order by 3.
Let the shift back be -3.
Say "Plain:  {the order}"
Say "Secret: {the hidden}"
Say "Again:  {the cipher of the hidden by the shift back}"
For example, the hidden is "dwwdfn dw gdzq, eb wkh rog eulgjh!".
For example, the cipher of the hidden by the shift back is "attack at dawn, by the old bridge!".

For example, the mirroring of "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama!" is yes.
For example, the mirroring of "A man, a plan, a canoe" is no.
Let the riddle be "Was it a car or a cat I saw?".
Say "Is ""{the riddle}"" a palindrome? {the mirroring of the riddle}."

# Counting: the words of a line, and how many are long.
Let the saying be "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".
Let the long ones be 0.
For each word in the words of the saying:
  If the length of the word is more than 4:
    Add 1 to the long ones.
Say "{the number of items in the words of the saying} words, {the long ones} of them longer than four letters."
If the saying contains "fox" and the saying starts with "the" and not the saying ends with "cat":
  Say "It mentions a fox, begins with ""the"", and does not end with a cat."

title: Roman numerals
note: Into numerals and back, with a table made of things.
source:
# Roman numerals, both ways.
#
# The table of numerals is a kind of thing. Going through the things in the
# order they were made, largest first, is the whole method.

A numeral has a worth (number) and a sign (text).

There is a numeral called Thousand whose worth is 1,000 and whose sign is "M".
There is a numeral called Ninehundred whose worth is 900 and whose sign is "CM".
There is a numeral called Fivehundred whose worth is 500 and whose sign is "D".
There is a numeral called Fourhundred whose worth is 400 and whose sign is "CD".
There is a numeral called Hundred whose worth is 100 and whose sign is "C".
There is a numeral called Ninety whose worth is 90 and whose sign is "XC".
There is a numeral called Fifty whose worth is 50 and whose sign is "L".
There is a numeral called Forty whose worth is 40 and whose sign is "XL".
There is a numeral called Ten whose worth is 10 and whose sign is "X".
There is a numeral called Nine whose worth is 9 and whose sign is "IX".
There is a numeral called Five whose worth is 5 and whose sign is "V".
There is a numeral called Four whose worth is 4 and whose sign is "IV".
There is a numeral called Unit whose worth is 1 and whose sign is "I".

# Into Roman: take the largest numeral that still fits, as often as it fits.
To work out the roman (text) of a year (number):
  Let the rest be the year.
  Let the line be "".
  For each numeral:
    While the rest is at least the numeral's worth:
      Set the line to "{the line}{the numeral's sign}".
      Subtract the numeral's worth from the rest.
  The answer is the line.

# What one Roman letter is worth, or nothing if it is not one.
To work out the weight (number, if any) of a mark (text):
  For each numeral whose sign is the mark:
    The answer is the numeral's worth.
  The answer is nothing.

# Out of Roman: add up the letters, but a letter that stands before a bigger
# one is taken away instead, as the I in IV is.
To work out the reading (number) of a line (text):
  Let the total be 0.
  Let the spot be 0.
  Let the size be the length of the line.
  Repeat the size times:
    Add 1 to the spot.
    Let the mark be the first 1 letters of the last (the size - the spot + 1) letters of the line.
    Let the here be the weight of the mark.
    If the here is nothing:
      Fail because "{the mark} is not a Roman numeral".
    Let the after be 0.
    If the spot is less than the size:
      Let the following be the first 1 letters of the last (the size - the spot) letters of the line.
      Set the after to the weight of the following or else 0.
    If the here is less than the after:
      Subtract the here from the total.
    Otherwise:
      Add the here to the total.
  The answer is the total.

For example, the roman of 1994 is "MCMXCIV".
For example, the roman of 3999 is "MMMCMXCIX".
For example, the reading of "MCMXCIV" is 1994.
For example, the reading of "XLII" is 42.

Say "2026 is {the roman of 2026}."
Say "1666 is {the roman of 1666}."
Let the date be "MDCLXVI".
Say "{the date} is {the reading of the date}."

title: A small bank
note: Money, percentages, a rule that is never broken, and Try.
source:
# A small bank: money, percentages, rules, and recovering from a refusal.

An account has a balance (money), a rate (percent), and a partner (account, if any).
An account can be frozen.

# No account may ever be overdrawn. This is checked on every change.
An account's balance is never less than $0.

# An account is thriving when it holds a good sum and nothing stands in its way.
An account is thriving when its balance is at least $1,000 and it is not frozen.

There is an account called Ada whose balance is $1,000 and whose rate is 5%.
There is an account called Bo whose balance is $40 and whose rate is 2%.
There is an account called Cy whose balance is $250 and whose rate is 3.5% and whose partner is Ada.

To pay an amount (money) from a giver (account) to a taker (account):
  If the giver is frozen:
    Fail because "{the giver}'s account is frozen".
  If the amount is at most $0:
    Fail because "a payment has to be more than nothing".
  Add the amount to the taker's balance.
  Subtract the amount from the giver's balance.
  Say "{the giver} pays {the taker} {the amount}."

# A payment either happens whole or not at all: a failed Try puts the world back.
To attempt an amount (money) from a giver (account) to a taker (account):
  Try:
    Pay the amount from the giver to the taker.
  If that fails:
    Say "No payment from {the giver}: {the problem}"

Attempt $60 from Ada to Bo.
Attempt $500 from Bo to Ada.
For example, Ada's balance is $940 and Bo's balance is $100.

Now Cy is frozen.
Attempt $10 from Cy to Bo.
Now Cy is not frozen.
Attempt $0 from Cy to Bo.

# A year's interest, ten years running. "5% of" a sum is a sum.
Repeat 10 times:
  For each account:
    Add the account's rate of the account's balance to the account's balance.

For each account:
  If the account has a partner:
    Say "{the account} has {the account's balance}, and shares with {the account's partner}."
  Otherwise:
    Say "{the account} has {the account's balance}."

Say "Thriving: {the number of thriving accounts} of {the number of accounts}."
Say "The bank holds {the total balance of all accounts}."

# $940 at 5% for ten years, to the cent.
For example, Ada's balance is more than $1,531.16 and Ada's balance is less than $1,531.17.

title: The Game of Life
note: Forty-nine cells, each a thing, and a glider that walks.
source:
# Conway's Game of Life, on a small board.
#
# Each cell is alive or dead. At every tick, a live cell with two or three live
# neighbours stays alive, a dead cell with exactly three comes alive, and every
# other cell is dead. A "glider" is five cells that walk across the board.

A cell has a row (number) and a column (number).
A cell can be alive.
A cell can be chosen.

Let the size always be 7.

# Make the board, a row at a time.
Let the across be 0.
Let the down be 0.
Repeat the size times:
  Add 1 to the down.
  Set the across to 0.
  Repeat the size times:
    Add 1 to the across.
    There is a new cell whose row is the down and whose column is the across.

To wake a rank (number) by a file (number):
  For each cell whose row is the rank:
    If the cell's column is the file:
      Now the cell is alive.

# How many of the eight cells around a cell are alive.
To work out the company (number) of a cell:
  Let the count be 0.
  For each other in alive cells:
    Let the rows apart be the other's row - the cell's row.
    Let the columns apart be the other's column - the cell's column.
    If the rows apart is at least -1 and the rows apart is at most 1 and the columns apart is at least -1 and the columns apart is at most 1:
      If the other is not the cell:
        Add 1 to the count.
  The answer is the count.

# One tick. Every cell is judged by the board as it stands, so the choice is
# marked first and only then carried out.
To tick:
  For each cell:
    Let the near be the company of the cell.
    If the near is 3 or (the near is 2 and the cell is alive):
      Now the cell is chosen.
    Otherwise:
      Now the cell is not chosen.
  For each cell:
    If the cell is chosen:
      Now the cell is alive.
    Otherwise:
      Now the cell is not alive.

To show:
  Set the down to 0.
  Repeat the size times:
    Add 1 to the down.
    Let the line be "".
    For each cell whose row is the down:
      If the cell is alive:
        Set the line to "{the line}# ".
      Otherwise:
        Set the line to "{the line}. ".
    Say the line.
  Say ""

# A glider in the top corner.
Wake 1 by 2.
Wake 2 by 3.
Wake 3 by 1.
Wake 3 by 2.
Wake 3 by 3.

Say "At the start:"
Show.
Repeat 4 times:
  Tick.
Say "After four ticks, the same shape, one step down and one across:"
Show.

For example, the number of alive cells is 5.
For example, the number of alive cells whose row is 4 is 3.

title: An almanac, from the chapters of a book
note: It uses three chapters of the almanac book: a calendar, Roman numerals and the feasts of the year.
source:
# An almanac for a year, put together from the chapters of a book.
#
# A chapter is a file, and a book is a folder of them. The book used here is
# the folder "almanac" beside this file. Each of its chapters says at the top
# which of its words it shares, and this program can use those and no others.

Use the calendar chapter of the almanac book.
Use the numerals chapter of the almanac book.
Use the feasts chapter of the almanac book.

Let the year be 2027.

Say "An Almanack for the Year {the roman of the year},"
If the leapness of the year is yes:
  Say "being a leap year of 366 days."
Otherwise:
  Say "being a common year of 365 days."
Say ""

For each feast:
  Say "{the feast} falls on a {the falling of the feast for the year}, {the feast's day} {the month title of the feast's month}."

Say ""
Say "{the number of wintry feasts} of the {the number of feasts} fall in the cold months."
Say "February has {the month length of 2 for the year} days, and Michaelmas is in {the month title of Michaelmas's month}."

For example, the reading of "MMXXVII" is the year.
For example, the falling of Michaelmas for the year is "Wednesday".

title: A to-do list for the web
note: The program behind “A page”, in four chapters of the tasks book. Run it, and its page appears under what it says.
source:
# A to-do list for the web, put together from the chapters of a book.
#
# With the page library, a thing is an element of the page. Making a card puts
# a line on the page; ticking the box on the page makes the card "ticked" here.
# Nothing in this program touches the page directly: it only changes things,
# and says what to do whenever a person changes them.
#
# The work is in four chapters of the book "tasks", a folder beside this file:
#
#   layout    what is on the page
#   cards     what a task is, and how one is written down
#   showing   which cards are in sight, and the counts
#   keeping   what is remembered between visits
#
# This file is what is left: what happens whenever a person does something.
# Open docs/todo.html to use it. Run from the command line, it sketches the page.

Use the page library.
Use the layout chapter of the tasks book.
Use the cards chapter of the tasks book.
Use the showing chapter of the tasks book.
Use the keeping chapter of the tasks book.

# Bring everything up to date. Each step is one chapter's work.
To tidy:
  Arrange.
  Sift.
  Reckon.
  Keep.

# Write down what was typed. If it cannot be written down, say why, and leave
# what was typed where it is: a failed Try puts everything back.
To take a line (text):
  Try:
    Jot the line.
    Set Entry's wording to "".
    Set Notice's wording to "".
  If that fails:
    Set Notice's wording to "Not added: {the problem}."
  Tidy.

# -------------------------------------------------------- as the page opens

Fetch.
Favour Everything for "all".
Tidy.

# ------------------------------------------------ what happens from here on

Whenever Adder becomes pressed:
  Take Entry's wording.

Whenever Entry becomes entered:
  Take Entry's wording.

Whenever a card becomes ticked:
  Tidy.

Whenever a card becomes not ticked:
  Tidy.

Whenever a card becomes starred:
  Tidy.

Whenever a card becomes not starred:
  Tidy.

# A card's words can be edited where they stand. Rubbing them all out removes it.
Whenever a card becomes reworded:
  If the card's wording is "":
    Shelve the card.
  Tidy.

Whenever a card becomes dismissed:
  Set Notice's wording to """{the card's wording}"" was removed."
  Shelve the card.
  Tidy.

Whenever Restorer becomes pressed:
  Restore.
  Set Notice's wording to "".
  Tidy.

Whenever Finder becomes changed:
  Sift.

Whenever Everything becomes pressed:
  Favour Everything for "all".
  Tidy.

Whenever Waiting becomes pressed:
  Favour Waiting for "open".
  Tidy.

Whenever Finished becomes pressed:
  Favour Finished for "done".
  Tidy.

Whenever Finisher becomes pressed:
  For each open card:
    Now the card is ticked.
  Tidy.

Whenever Sweeper becomes pressed:
  For each ticked card:
    Shelve the card.
  Tidy.
